\subsection{Main comparison}
\resulttable{CIC17_main_b010_paper.tex}{CIC-IDS2017, label budget 10\%, delay 1 window.}{tab:cic17}
\resulttable{IDS18_main_b010_paper.tex}{CSE-CIC-IDS2018, label budget 10\%, delay 1 window.}{tab:ids18}
\resulttable{UNSW_main_b010_paper.tex}{UNSW-NB15 (four classes held out of training), label budget 10\%.}{tab:unsw}

\textbf{CIC-IDS2017} (\cref{tab:cic17}). \nova{} and CBRS replay tie on OW-F1 (0.752 against 0.755). \nova{}
has the higher AUT (0.860 against 0.837), but the per-window difference is within the bootstrap uncertainty
($+2.2$ points, 95\% CI $[-0.3, +4.6]$), and \nova{} varies more across seeds (0.721 to 0.776 against 0.752 to
0.757). It is significantly ahead of every other method (by 7.0 to 23.1 points). CBRS detects slightly more
attacks (detection F1 0.863 against 0.858), but \nova{} flags significantly fewer benign flows (2.8\% against
4.5\% pooled; per-window difference $-4.2$, CI $[-9.0, -0.4]$): it sends 38\% fewer benign flows to the analyst.

\textbf{CSE-CIC-IDS2018} (\cref{tab:ids18}). \nova{} and CBRS replay tie on OW-F1 (0.738 against 0.730) and AUT
(0.867 against 0.870; difference CI $[-2.3, +1.4]$). \nova{} has the higher detection F1 (0.803 against 0.784), a
significantly lower false-positive rate (3.2\% against 4.7\%; CI $[-5.5, -0.4]$) and four times less forgetting
(0.008 against 0.032).

\textbf{UNSW-NB15} (\cref{tab:unsw}, \cref{fig:time-unsw}). Most adaptive methods end \emph{below} the static
model (0.499); CBRS replay reaches 0.326. They learn Exploits and Fuzzers, but every later flow of these classes is
rejected as \unk{}: the thresholds were calibrated on January traffic, and February flows of the same classes lie
outside them. \nova{} recalibrates learned classes on its calibration store and reaches 0.511 OW-F1 and 0.596
AUT, significantly ahead of every replay-based method ($+19.6$ to $+29.4$ points) and level with the static model
($+2.7$, CI $[-0.0, +4.9]$), with the highest detection F1 (0.858) and lowest false-positive rate (6.7\% against
7.5--19.0\%). On the classes the model knows, \nova{} reaches a macro-F1 of 0.505 against at most 0.165 for any
other method. Without the calibration store, \nova{} drops to 0.418 and zero F1 on Exploits and Fuzzers
(\cref{tab:ablation}), confirming the mechanism.

INSOMNIA's self-training has the highest false-positive rate on both CIC datasets (12.4\%, 25.8\%):
pseudo-label errors on unseen classes are fed back into training.

\Cref{fig:time-cic} shows where the methods differ on CIC-IDS2017. Every method drops when a new attack class
starts. CBRS replay recovers faster from the first DoS attacks (windows 8--12), \nova{} from most later ones,
most visibly in the last ten windows.

\subsection{Label budget}
With 1\% of each window labelled (\cref{tab:budget}), \nova{} leads CBRS replay by 8.5 points on CIC-IDS2017
(per-window $+5.7$, CI $[+1.4, +10.2]$) and by 1.8 points on CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (CI $[-0.0, +4.7]$, not
significant). On UNSW-NB15 it trails periodic retraining (0.470 against 0.501; per-window $-5.0$, CI
$[-10.3, -0.9]$). With 40 labels per window, periodic retraining never
collects enough labels of the held-out classes to learn them, so it keeps rejecting them as \unk{}, which the
metric credits in full. Its macro-F1 on the classes the model knows is only 0.150, against 0.390 for \nova{}, which
names 62\% of known attack flows correctly against 6\%. \nova{} learns DoS and Reconnaissance, which overlap with
Exploits, and loses the \unk{} credit; open-world macro-F1 alone cannot separate ``never learned'' from ``learned
imperfectly''. \nova{} also has the lowest false-positive rate (10.7\% against $\geq$16.2\%).

On CIC-IDS2017 every removal lowers OW-F1 (\cref{tab:ablation}), most for the guard ($-5.6$, in every seed). The
loss is concentrated in XSS and Bot: without the guard, models that name XSS flows Brute Force are deployed, whereas
with it XSS stays \unk{} and receives full open-world credit. Per window, no single removal is significant on
CIC-IDS2017. On UNSW-NB15 the guard and the calibration store are essential ($-22.1$, $-9.1$); both variants lose
Exploits and Fuzzers. On CSE-CIC-IDS2018 the stream-level changes have inconsistent signs across seeds, because four
of its classes have only 2 to 33 flows. Per window, only the query and propagation help significantly there
(block-bootstrap CIs $[-3.1, -0.3]$ and $[-3.6, -0.5]$). Replacing the class-conditional $k$-NN detector by
distance to the nearest class centroid (three seeds) lowers OW-F1 from 0.768 to 0.712 for \nova{} and from 0.311
to 0.178 for the static model, which then labels almost every attack benign: one centroid cannot follow multi-modal benign
traffic.

\textbf{Neural classifier.} With an MLP instead of gradient boosting on CIC-IDS2017, \nova{} keeps the lowest
false-positive rate (3.3\% against 4.7\%), the higher detection F1 and an equal AUT, but its OW-F1 is lower than
CBRS replay's (0.622 against 0.711), mainly on two short-lived web attacks. We do not claim that its accuracy
advantage carries over to neural classifiers.
